stances.claim: The JBC's nomination process has been transparent, accountable, and dignified -- live TV coverage and probing questions without loss of decency or civility.

Body language, tone, voice inflection, and facial expressions in JBC interviews often reveal more than verbal answers -- the people can now assess responsiveness, mental dexterity, and innate personality.
There are no partisan blocs or permanent alliances in the SC -- those voting together in one case may be miles apart in the next, which is how it should be.

The SC operates like a corporate board of directors -- the CJ is CEO but needs the 14 other justices; administrative supervision is delegated through a comprehensive resolution (AM 99-12-08-SC, 2003).

notable_anecdotes: Sereno during her JBC interview explaining to acting chair J. Peralta that there are no partisan blocs or permanent alliances in the SC -- one of the most direct insider disclosures about the Court's internal dynamics.

The 10-minute debate threshold: when a single agenda item discussion exceeds 10 minutes, the CJ typically postpones and asks protagonists to submit written arguments -- a discipline that keeps 200+ item sessions functional.
The AM 99-12-08-SC (April 22, 2003) comprehensive delegation resolution -- the 15-justice board-of-directors governance model that allows the SC to supervise 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees.

The reader's question: 'How can a collegial body supervise a nationwide institution?' -- answered through the corporate board analogy: the SC en banc acts as the board; the CJ is the CEO; divisions and the executive committee handle delegated powers.

decision_framework_signals: Use public JBC interviews as the primary transparency mechanism -- body language and demeanor are as important as verbal answers
Accept that SC voting patterns are issue-by-issue, not bloc-driven -- don't predict outcomes by perceived alliances
Apply the board-of-directors model: delegate routine administration to executive committee, divisions, and CJ; reserve en banc for policy-level and disciplinary decisions
Require all judicial candidates to submit SALN, ITR, and bank waivers as baseline transparency -- the JBC's 2012 precedent
one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers a mid-process assessment of the JBC's nomination process -- transparent, accountable, and dignified -- noting that live TV and radio coverage allowed the public to observe 20 candidates under probing but civil questioning by JBC members. Body language, voice inflection, facial expression, and eye contact often revealed more than verbal answers -- 'Tinimbang sila at hindi naman nagkulang.' Though 20 candidates was too many (some outsiders had no real chance), the JBC also weighed education, track record, past decisions, SALNs, ITRs, and bank records. He highlights two SC peculiarities the interviews revealed. First, Sereno explained to acting chair J. Peralta that there are no partisan blocs or permanent alliances in the SC -- those voting together in one case may be miles apart in the next; 200+ agenda items per session with the 10-minute debate threshold before issues are referred to written argument. Second, a reader asks how 15 justices can supervise 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees: the author answers through the corporate board analogy -- the SC en banc acts as the board of directors, guided by A.M. No. 99-12-08-SC (April 22, 2003), which delegates: the executive committee (CJ + top two senior) handles personnel appointments and court committees; the three divisions handle inhibitions, extensions, venue transfers, and routine discipline (short of dismissal); the CJ handles detailing of personnel, overtime, and procurement. The CJ is the CEO but needs the 14 other justices as 'the board of directors.'
